summary:
The research team gathered at More Up Campus in Montgomery, Alabama, home of Michelle Browder’s Mothers of Gynecology monument to Anarcha, Lucy and Betsey. It was the project’s first time together in the place where J. Marion Sims operated on them in the 1840s.
We walked and listened near where Anarcha lived, stood at the marker for Sims’s office and at the monument to the women he experimented on, and took part in a speculative storytelling workshop led by the librettist Deborah D.E.E.P. Mouton. DW McCrary filmed throughout for the documentary.
The aim was to listen to the place before writing anything for it: to let the land, the buildings and one another shape the questions the opera and the research will carry.

A visit to Provincetown, Massachusetts, to spend time with Professor Evelynn Hammonds, historian of science and medicine at Harvard University and a Project Associate.
Her work on race, gender and the history of medicine is a long-standing touchstone for this project. The visit was a chance to think alongside her about the archive, absence, and what it means to listen to history.

We travelled to New York to read the institutional record of this history: the papers and collections through which Sims’s work became medicine. We worked in the collections of the New York Academy of Medicine and the Arthur H. Aufses, Jr. MD Archives at Mount Sinai Hospital.
The goal was not to recover Anarcha’s voice from documents that never held it. It was to understand how the record was made, what it chose to keep, and where its silences are. What we found will inform the libretto, the project’s critical framework and the documentary.
